title: Words that make words
goal: Build and recognise nouns from roots you already know: *pe-* for the person who does it, *pe-an* and *per-an* for the doing, *ke-an* for abstract ideas and *-an* for the thing that results. With these five patterns, one root can give you half a dozen words.
bekal: name people by what they do: *pembeli, penjual, pengajar, pembicara*
follow an office meeting full of nouns: *pendaftaran, perjalanan, pelatihan, kebutuhan*
read and write a simple shop sign: *makanan, minuman, pesanan, kebersihan*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rapat program pelatihan
dialogs.intro: Monday, nine o'clock, the small meeting room of the Yogyakarta office. Mbak Nur chairs the first planning meeting for an English training programme for teachers from the partner schools.

lines.speaker: Nur:
lines.text: Baik, kita mulai. Agenda hari ini persiapan program pelatihan guru.

lines.literal: good, we begin. agenda day this preparation programme training teacher.

lines.text: Betul. Ada tiga puluh peserta dari enam sekolah. Pendaftarannya dibuka minggu depan.

lines.text: Mas Bayu, fokus. Tapi ya, makan siang dan kudapan juga kita sediakan.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Setuju, Mbak. Formulir pendaftarannya saya siapkan hari ini juga.

notes: **Baik, kita mulai.** Mbak Nur's meeting opener is the standard one: *Baik* (right), then *kita mulai* or, a notch more formal, *mari kita mulai*. *Agenda hari ini…* follows with a noun, never a verb — meetings in Indonesian are made of nouns, which is exactly why this unit exists.

**Peserta** (participant) is a *pe-* word from *serta*, “to take part, go along with”. You will see it everywhere: on name tags, forms and certificates. The whole group is *para peserta*, “the participants”, in speeches and emails.

**Ditanggung kantor.** *Menanggung* is to bear or to cover a cost; *ditanggung kantor* is “covered by the office”. As in Unit 6, the doer comes straight after the *di-* verb without *oleh*. It is a phrase worth knowing before you book anything.

**Kudapan** is the formal word for snacks, used in invitations and budgets. 💬 In conversation people say *camilan*, or simply *snack*, and a box of cakes at a meeting is a *snack box* or *nasi kotak* if there is rice in it.
**Siap!** — literally “ready!”, from the army, and now the standard office answer to an instruction: “will do, on it”. Say it to your boss with a straight face and you will sound entirely local.

**Keahlian, semoga.** *Ahli* is an expert; *keahlian* is expertise. Mas Bayu's desk is famously a mess, so his claim is a joke, and Mbak Nur's one-word answer *Semoga* — “let's hope so” — is the driest reply available in the language.

grammars.title: pe- and pe-an: the doer and the doing
body: Take a *me-* verb, swap *me-* for *pe-* (with the same sound changes), and you get the person who does it. Add *-an* as well and you get the act or process. The table runs from verb to doer to doing.
after: The nasal sound of *pe-* follows *me-* exactly: *mem-/pem-, men-/pen-, meng-/peng-, meny-/peny-*. If you can build the *me-* verb from Units 2 and 3, you can build the *pe-* noun.
⚠️ *Melatih* gives *pelatih* and *pelatihan*, not *pemlatih*: roots beginning with *l, m, n, r, w, y* take plain *pe-*, just as they take plain *me-*.

grammars.title: per-an, ke-an and -an
body: Three more patterns turn roots into nouns. Each has a typical meaning, although you will always meet exceptions.

head: Pattern
Usually means
Examples
rows: the activity or its result, often from *ber-* verbs

after: *Perjalanan* comes from *berjalan*, *pertemuan* from *bertemu*: that is the typical source of *per-an* nouns. *Pelatihan* and *pendaftaran*, from *me-* verbs, take *pe-an*. It is not a watertight rule, but it will make your guesses right most of the time.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Papan nama warung
dialogs.intro: Saturday afternoon. Bu Endang runs a small food stall at the front of her house, and a sign painter has left her a new board to check. She calls Sarah over to read it.

notes: **Tulisan** is “writing, what is written”, from *tulis* + *-an*: the result of writing. It is also the word for handwriting (*tulisannya bagus*) and for an article (*tulisan saya di koran*).
**Sedia** on a sign means “available, we have”. Signs and menus love short noun lists: *Sedia: pulsa, gas, air galon*. You met its relatives *menyediakan* and *disediakan* in A1.

**Arisan, pengajian.** An *arisan* is a regular social gathering, usually of women, where everyone pays into a pot and one member wins it each time. A *pengajian* (from *kaji*, to study) is a Koran-reading or religious study meeting. Both need food, which is where Bu Endang comes in.

**Makin banyak** — “more and more”. *Makin* (formal *semakin*) before an adjective means increasing: *makin mahal*, *makin ramai*. 💬 *Pinter* is the Javanese-flavoured pronunciation of *pintar*, clever.

**Gorengan, mendoan.** *Gorengan* (from *goreng*, fry) is the whole family of fried snacks: tofu, tempeh, battered vegetables, bananas. *Mendoan* is thin tempeh dipped in spiced batter and fried only briefly, so it stays soft; it comes from Banyumas in Central Java.
**Mbak bisa aja** — “oh, you!”. The standard reply to a compliment you are pleased about but too polite to accept. Literally “you can just (say that)”. 💬 *Aja* is the spoken *saja*.

grammars.title: -an: the thing that results
body: Plain *-an* on a verb root usually gives you the object or result of the action: what you eat, what you order, what you fry. These are among the most frequent nouns in the language.
after: Compare *pesanan* (the order, the thing ordered) with *pemesanan* (the ordering, the booking process): *Pesanan Anda sudah siap* — your order is ready; *Pemesanan tiket bisa lewat aplikasi* — tickets can be booked through the app. The longer word is the process, the shorter one the thing.

blocks.text: The real payoff of affixes is that you can see a family at a glance. Here is everything Indonesian builds from *ajar*, “teach, instruct”. You already know half of it.
Notice the two branches: *pelajar* and *pelajaran* come from *belajar* (learning), *pengajar* and *pengajaran* from *mengajar* (teaching). The prefix of the noun remembers which verb it came from.
Wrap *ke-…-an* round an adjective and you get the abstract noun, the English “-ness” or “-ity”. These are the words of signs, slogans and speeches.

blocks.title: Nouns you will read on walls
items: *Kebersihan sebagian dari iman.* — Cleanliness is part of faith (on mosques, schools and toilets).
